A four-stroke engine turns the energy stored in fuel into useful mechanical work by repeating a simple cycle four times for every full rotation of the crankshaft. The “four strokes” are the four movements of the piston inside the cylinder: **intake**, **compression**, **power**, and **exhaust**.

The piston moves up and down in the cylinder. It is connected to a connecting rod, which pushes and pulls on the **crankshaft**. The crankshaft converts the piston’s straight up-and-down motion into continuous rotation. That rotation is what ultimately drives the wheels, propeller, generator, or other machinery.

Valves control the flow of gases into and out of the cylinder. In a basic petrol engine, there is usually an **intake valve** and an **exhaust valve**. The valves open and close at precise times so that fresh charge can enter, the mixture can be compressed, the expanding gases can push the piston, and the spent gases can be expelled.
